final_proof:
As stated, the claim is not a well-posed consequence of the hypotheses if “discrete set of subsets” has its standard topological meaning: no topology on X, and no hypothesis connecting the relations V_k to neighborhoods, is given. In fact, even after X is equipped with a topology, the stated hypotheses alone do not imply the claim. What they do imply is the following precise relation-theoretic statement:

For every n>0 and every p∈X, the set V_{n+2}[p] meets at most one member of the collection A_n. Consequently, the advertised conclusion is true under the natural additional hypothesis that every V_k[p] is a neighborhood of p (for a fixed n, it suffices that every V_{n+2}[p] be a neighborhood of p).

For a relation R, write R[x]={z∈X:(x,z)∈R}, and use the convention

(R∘S)[x]=⋃_{t∈S[x]}R[t].

Thus U_{n+1}=V_{n+1}∘U_n.

Proof of the corrected statement. Fix n>0. We first show that if x and y are distinct, then no point of A_n(x) is V_{n+1}-related to a point of A_n(y). Because the well-order is total, either x≺y or y≺x. Suppose first that x≺y. If a∈A_n(x), b∈A_n(y), and (a,b)∈V_{n+1}, then a∈U_n[x], and hence

b∈(V_{n+1}∘U_n)[x]=U_{n+1}[x].

But x≺y, and the definition of A_n(y) removes U_{n+1}[z] for every z≺y. In particular it removes U_{n+1}[x], contradicting b∈A_n(y). If y≺x, symmetry of V_{n+1} changes (a,b)∈V_{n+1} into (b,a)∈V_{n+1}, and the same argument with x and y interchanged again gives a contradiction. Therefore

(A_n(x)×A_n(y))∩V_{n+1}=∅ whenever x≠y.  (1)

Now fix p∈X. Suppose V_{n+2}[p] met two distinct members B and C of A_n. Choose

a∈V_{n+2}[p]∩B,  b∈V_{n+2}[p]∩C,

and choose x,y∈X such that B=A_n(x) and C=A_n(y). Since B and C are distinct, x≠y. We have (p,a),(p,b)∈V_{n+2}. By symmetry, (a,p)∈V_{n+2}; hence

(a,b)∈V_{n+2}∘V_{n+2}⊆V_{n+1},

contradicting (1). Thus V_{n+2}[p] meets at most one member of A_n.

If X has a topology and each V_{n+2}[p] is a neighborhood of p, choose an open neighborhood O_p of p contained in V_{n+2}[p]. Then O_p also meets at most one member of A_n. Since this holds for every p∈X, A_n is a discrete collection in the standard topological sense.

Finally, the missing neighborhood assumption cannot simply be omitted. Let X={0,1} have the indiscrete topology, well-ordered by 0≺1, and put V_k=Δ_X for every k∈N. All the stated relation hypotheses hold, and U_n=Δ_X for every n. Consequently,

A_n(0)={0},  A_n(1)={1},

so A_n={{0},{1}}. The only neighborhood of either point is X, which meets both members; hence this collection is not discrete. Thus the original topological claim is false as written, while the additional neighborhood hypothesis above gives a sufficient correction.
